# Chapter 1: The Pour

The crucible is already at temperature when I close my hands around the tongs.

Heat presses against my face like a flat palm. The bellows behind me exhale in slow, mechanical pulls — a sound I have memorized the way other people memorize their own heartbeat — and the forge light throws everything orange and unsteady. I do not look at Kellan. I know he is there. I know where he stands: three paces back, left of the anvil block, arms crossed, the Registry ledger tucked under his elbow. He has stood in that exact position twice before while I failed.

I will not think about the twice before.

The sequence begins with the draw. I pull the crucible from the cradle in a single controlled arc, no hesitation, wrists locked at the angle Kellan drilled into me through six months of correction. The metal inside is molten and pale gold, and it moves the way water moves when it is trying not to spill — slow on the surface, urgent underneath. First failure was a wrist break on the draw. Second was a premature tilt. My body remembers both of them the way a foot remembers a bad step on a dark stair.

Not this time.

The tilt comes at count four. I have counted it in my sleep, in the yard, eating breakfast. The metal begins its pour into the mold at the angle the Registry form specifies — thirty degrees, sustained, no correction mid-flow. My arms are shaking with the weight, but they are shaking correctly, within the range that does not constitute a fault. I know the difference. I have had time to learn the difference.

Kellan says nothing. That is not unusual.

The pour runs clean for seven counts. Then something happens that I do not have a name for.

The metal in the mold shifts color. Not the gradual darkening of cooling — I know that, I have watched it a hundred times — but a lateral change, a seam of deeper red opening across the surface like a crack in old wood, then closing, then holding still. The smell changes too: the usual char and iron-bite replaced for one breath by something almost sweet, almost organic, before it vanishes back into smoke.

"Well," I say, not stopping the pour, "that's new." My voice comes out lighter than I mean it to, pitched for a laugh Kellan is never going to give me. Nobody laughs. The mold keeps taking metal.

I do not stop. Stopping is an automatic procedural fault. I have already failed twice; I will not hand Kellan a third mark before the metal even cools. I complete the pour. I set the crucible down. I step back to the line and put my hands at my sides.

The forge breathes. The bellows pull and push.

Kellan uncrosses his arms. He steps forward and looks at the mold for a long time. He does not open the ledger. He does not write anything. He looks at me once — not the way a judge looks at a result, but the way a man looks at a thing he does not yet have a category for — and then he says, "You're dismissed."

No pass. No fail. Nothing written.

From the corner of the forge, Merin is watching me with an expression I have never seen on their face before.
